description: We are a 2-person multidisciplinary squad combining data & science analysis, software development, visual design, and video storytelling. Excited to tackle NASA's 2026 challenges and build an impactful, data-driven mission prototype together!
summary:
Lunar Horizon is a website we built to help pick where and when to land near the Moon's south pole. A lander there needs sunlight for its solar panels and a view of Earth to send data home. Because the Sun stays close to the horizon at the pole, a mountain tens of kilometres away can put a site in shadow for days or hide the Earth.

We used NASA's LRO elevation data to work out the actual horizon around each site, then calculated where the Sun and Earth are every hour. We checked those positions against NASA JPL Horizons and they agree to within 0.004°. You can pick from points in the Artemis candidate regions, the Apollo and CLPS landing sites and other countries' landers, or type in your own coordinates. It shows how often each one gets sun and Earth contact, the longest dark stretch, when you can land, and what changes if the landing date slips. Each site gets a score and a verdict, you can put any two side by side, and there's a 3D view of the terrain.

We wanted something a mission planner could use, but that a student could also open and understand.
details:
Lunar Horizon is a website for comparing lunar landing sites and dates. For any site it shows when there's enough sunlight for solar power and when the Earth is above the terrain for radio contact. Near the south pole, where Artemis plans to land, the Sun stays low, so distant mountains can cut off power or the view of Earth for days.

We use NASA's LOLA elevation data (240 m near the pole, 3.8 km elsewhere) to trace the real skyline around each site, then track the Sun and Earth against it hour by hour. Our positions match NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.004°.

You can pick sites from the Artemis candidate regions, Apollo, CLPS, Chang'e, Chandrayaan-3 and SLIM, or enter any coordinates. A south pole map and a whole-Moon map show which sites have sunlight and Earth contact right now. Each site has a 360° horizon view and a 3D terrain view with moving shadows. It also gets a row on a timeline of sunlight, Earth contact and landing times.

The analysis tabs include:

  • Compare sites: score out of 100, GO/CAUTION/NO-GO verdict, sunlight, Earth contact, longest darkness, solar power and battery needed for the night.
  • Head to head: any two sites side by side.
  • Date slips: what a delay of up to three months does at every site.
  • Landing windows: touchdown times that give a full surface stay in continuous sunlight.
  • Clearance over time: how far the Sun and Earth sit above the terrain.
  • Events and export: every sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset, plus CSV downloads.
  • Nearby scan: suggests a better spot within 3 km.

You can change the assumptions, like equipment height and stay length, and share the exact setup with a link. It runs in any browser, including on phones.

We wanted it to help planners compare sites quickly, and to help students and the public see why the pole is so hard to land on.

We built it with TypeScript, React, three.js and Astronomy Engine, prepared the terrain with Python, and host it on Vercel. We used Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, to help write the code.

We checked every preset coordinate against published sources and the terrain, and the app is upfront about what a 240 m grid can't show.
